summary.text: A variable is a symbol, usually a letter, that stands for an unspecified mathematical object, often a number.
It can be an unknown that has to be found, or a parameter that stays fixed while a problem is worked on.
Viete began using letters for known and unknown numbers in the late 1500s, and Descartes set x, y and z for unknowns.

paragraphs.heading: A symbol for something unnamed
paragraphs.text: A variable is a symbol, usually a letter, that stands for a mathematical object which has not been pinned down. The word comes from the Latin variabilis, meaning changeable. Any object that could properly fill the role is called a value of the variable. The values tend to be of one kind, often numbers, and may form a set such as the real numbers. Sometimes no valid value exists, or it is not clear whether one does.

paragraphs.heading: An impossible pair
paragraphs.text: Suppose p and q stand for two integers, and we demand that the square of p be twice the square of q, written p² = 2 q². When p and q must be nonzero integers, no choice works. Proving that is not obvious, yet it has been known since ancient times. The result has strongly shaped mathematics ever since.

paragraphs.heading: Unknowns and parameters
paragraphs.text: At first the word mostly meant the argument of a function, whose value could be pictured as varying across the function's domain, and that is where the name comes from. Variables also stand for a function's values, like y in y = f(x); in that equation f is the function and x is its argument. A variable that stays fixed while a problem is being worked out is often called a parameter. One whose value has to be found is called an unknown. In the quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0, the letters a, b and c are parameters and x is the unknown.

paragraphs.heading: Early unknowns
paragraphs.text: Unknown quantities go back at least to ancient Egypt. The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus, from around 1500 BC, set out problems with unknowns in words; these are called the Aha problems, with aha meaning stack. Each asks for a quantity when its sum with parts of itself is given. Problem 19, for instance, wants a quantity that, taken one and a half times and added to 4, makes 10, which today reads 3/2x + 4 = 10. Mathematics in Mesopotamia's Old Babylonian period, around the same time, was more advanced and also dealt with quadratic and cubic equations.

paragraphs.heading: Letters take over
paragraphs.text: Near the end of the 16th century, François Viète had the idea of using letters for both known and unknown numbers, and of computing with those letters as if they were numbers. His rule was consonants for known values and vowels for unknowns. In 1637, René Descartes began writing unknowns as x, y and z and knowns as a, b and c. Unlike Viète's scheme, Descartes' version is still in common use.

paragraphs.heading: From changing to fixed
paragraphs.text: From the 1660s, Isaac Newton and, separately, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed calculus, which looks at how a tiny change in one quantity causes a change in another that depends on it. Almost a century later, Leonhard Euler introduced the notation y = f(x). Until the end of the 19th century, variable meant almost only the arguments and values of functions. Then Karl Weierstrass swapped the loose idea of a limit for a formal definition in which none of the variables is thought of as moving. That static view gave the modern meaning: a symbol for an object that is either unknown or can be replaced by any member of a given set.
